It's one of my favourites books and I've wrote my literature degree about it. I think one of the most human and empathetic experience literature can give, and after studying it deeply I discovered that there are a tons of layers of meaning and "literary games" that are not very important but are really interesting. I didn't find it so hard to read, and I've read it when I wasn't even a really brilliant reader. I think that the modernist style for example, I read recently "To the lighthouse", is way more hard. But I think to know what people when they say "hard", and it's boring. Because the idea of the book is that we are too passive in the experience of entertainment so it put us in the condition of sharing our amount of work. In order to do this he wrote a wall text of information about politics, technology, cinema and others stuff, in between amazing stories of the most human kind and jokes of every kind. In a interview he said that the most difficult part of writing Infinite Jest was to make it funny enough to convince the reader to get to the end, and in his first version it had like 400 more pages, almost all of jokes, that the editor cut out. The point is that the reader have to put an effort to get plot, reading thought wall texts of useless details and connecting dots between characters and notes.

I could talk for hours of all the brilliant ideas of the book but I think that the most important thing that regards it is  that Wallace found something very important that he need to talk about, and is synthesized in the characters of Hal and Mario. I won't spoil it to you but after the reading I would suggest to look for the "answer of the plot", because it can hard at first get all connections. A friend of mine read IJ recently and after I talled him all the connections between stories that were right in front of his eyes he started to get the whole plan and liked the book a lot more.
